passage:
Monday: Thomas watched the swing all lunch break. Class 3 had only one swing that worked, and he had been fourth in line when the bell rang.

Tuesday: This time he was second. Riya's brother jumped off, and Thomas stepped forward, but Yogesh slid onto the seat from the other side. Something hot shot up Thomas's neck. "That's MINE!" he shouted, so loudly the kids at the slide turned. "You saw me waiting! You did it on purpose!" Yogesh blinked and gripped the chains.

Wednesday: Thomas still felt the heat when he walked past the swing. At lunch Yogesh said quietly, "I didn't see a line. I was behind the tree." Thomas folded his arms. He wasn't sure he believed it yet.

qa.q: How many working swings did Class 3 have?
qa.a: Class 3 had only one swing that worked.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when Yogesh slid onto the seat?
qa.a: He felt a hot rush of unfairness and anger, and was sure Yogesh had taken the turn on purpose.

qa.q: What could help Thomas at this early stage, before it turns into a bigger fight?
qa.a: Taking a breath and asking Yogesh whether he saw the line, instead of shouting, might have kept it small.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have felt when Thomas shouted at him?
qa.a: Yogesh was probably startled and confused, since he says he didn't even see the line.

grounding: Over three days a child feels a hot jolt of unfairness over the swing and shouts, sure the other child did it on purpose.

passage:
Anirban, come here, your Madhuri Dadi will tell you something about fighting with your sister.

When I was ten, my brother Nitin and I broke Ma's glass lamp. We were chasing each other round the courtyard. Ma came running, and at once I said, "He pushed me into it!"

Nitin shouted, "She started it! She always starts it!"

"You never let me play! You always cheat!"

We got louder and louder. Ma was standing right there, but neither of us looked at her. I was busy thinking up the next thing to say. So was Nitin. Neither of us heard a single word the other said.

Finally Ma sat down on the step and said nothing at all. That silence stopped us. Then she asked, "Who wants to sweep the glass?" We both did it together.

qa.q: What did Madhuri and Nitin break?
qa.a: They broke Ma's glass lamp.

qa.q: What was Madhuri thinking about during the shouting?
qa.a: She was busy thinking up the next thing to say to defend herself, feeling defensive and angry rather than listening.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Ma sitting down in silence; with no one to argue at, the children stopped, and sweeping together turned blame into a shared job.

qa.q: How might Nitin have felt while they were shouting?
qa.a: Nitin probably felt angry and blamed, just as busy defending himself and just as unheard.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood quarrel where each child told the story so only the other was at fault, with 'always' and 'never' and no listening.

The badminton game in the colony compound had started as fun. Then Rajni called Minakshi's shot "out" and six kids gathered to watch.

"It was IN," said Minakshi. "You always cheat. Like last month in hopscotch."

"That was different!"

Everyone was looking. Minakshi's face burned. She wanted to win this more than she wanted the point. "At least my mother doesn't shout so loud the whole building hears," she said.

Rajni went very quiet. Her racket slipped down to her side.

Someone said "Ooooh." Minakshi felt a quick flash of triumph, and then, right behind it, something cold in her stomach. She had meant it to hurt. She could see that it had.

Rajni turned and walked towards her building without a word.

qa.q: What did Rajni call Minakshi's shot?
qa.a: Rajni called Minakshi's shot "out".

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling right after the insult?
qa.a: She felt a quick flash of triumph followed by a cold, guilty feeling, seeing that her words really hurt Rajni.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do now to stop things getting worse?
qa.a: She could follow Rajni or find her later, say sorry for the words about her mother, and leave the shot argument aside.

qa.q: What is it like for Rajni to hear that insult in front of everyone?
qa.a: Rajni is deeply hurt and embarrassed, since something painful about her family was used against her with others watching.

grounding: With an audience watching, a child drags in an old grievance and insults a friend's family, caring more about winning than the game.

passage:
"Chinmay can't even catch a tennis ball," Uma said to the line outside the library. "That's why we lost the relay."

"I didn't drop it!"

"You did. Everyone saw. Right?"

A few kids nodded.

"Stop it, Uma."

"Or what? You'll cry again like in Class 3?"

Chinmay's heart was thumping in his ears. His face felt hot all the way to his hair. He opened his mouth and nothing sensible came out.

"See? He can't even answer."

"SHUT UP!" Chinmay flung his library book down on the floor and ran. He didn't stop until he was behind the water tank, breathing fast, fists shaking.

Mr Sequeira found him there. "Chinmay? Take a minute. Breathe with me." After a while Chinmay's hands stopped shaking.

qa.q: Where did Chinmay run to?
qa.a: He ran to behind the water tank.

qa.q: How can you tell Chinmay felt overwhelmed rather than choosing what to do?
qa.a: His heart thumped, his face burned, no sensible words came, and he flung the book and ran, which shows his body taking over.

qa.q: How did Mr Sequeira help, and what could come next?
qa.a: He helped Chinmay breathe and calm down first; later he could talk with both children about what was said.

qa.q: How might Uma see the moment when Chinmay ran off?
qa.a: Uma may have been surprised by how strongly he reacted, and perhaps felt a flicker of guilt or felt she had 'won'.

grounding: A child on the receiving end of teasing floods with a racing heart and hot face, throws a book and runs, with his body taking over.

passage:
Dear Diary,

Today Omkar and I had the biggest fight of Class 5. He said I copied his drawing for the competition. I didn't. I said he was a liar and he said I was one. We were both shouting and I was nearly crying.

Rawat Ma'am came. She didn't say who was right. She just said, "Dolma, go and fill your bottle. Omkar, walk to the gate and back." I was angry she didn't take my side.

When I came back I felt less hot. Ma'am sat with me first and asked what happened and how I felt. I said I felt blamed for nothing. Then she talked to Omkar alone.

I still don't like what he said. But my stomach doesn't hurt anymore.

Dolma

qa.q: What did Omkar say Dolma copied?
qa.a: Omkar said Dolma copied his drawing for the competition.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when Rawat Ma'am didn't take her side?
qa.a: Dolma felt angry and let down, wanting the teacher to say who was right.

qa.q: Why did Rawat Ma'am's approach work?
qa.a: She separated them and let each cool down first, then listened to each one's story and feelings, so they could talk calmly.

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt walking to the gate and back?
qa.a: Omkar was probably still angry at first but calmer by the end, ready to tell his side when Ma'am talked to him alone.

grounding: A teacher separates two children without ruling on who won, lets each cool down, then asks each for their version and feelings.

passage:
Saturday

Me and Zubin had a fight about carrom again today. He kept taking two turns when he pocketed the queen, and I shouted "You cheat!" and he shouted back.

We both went home. After lunch I felt less angry. I went to Zubin's building and we sat on the steps. I didn't say "you cheat." I said, "I felt cheated when you took two turns. I didn't know that rule." He said his grandpa plays it that way.

So we made our own rule. You get one extra turn only if you cover the queen. We wrote it on a paper and stuck it under the board.

Then we played three games. I lost two. It was fine. I felt lighter, like after a big drink of water.

Vijay

qa.q: Where did Vijay and Zubin stick their rule?
qa.a: They stuck it on a paper under the board.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling after they agreed the rule and played?
qa.a: Vijay felt lighter and relieved, like after a big drink of water, even after losing two games.

qa.q: Which choice changed the argument, and why?
qa.a: Saying "I felt cheated" instead of "You cheat" helped Zubin explain his grandpa's rule, so they could agree what was fair.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt when Vijay came to his building?
qa.a: Zubin was probably relieved and more willing to explain calmly, since Vijay spoke about feelings instead of blaming.

grounding: After cooling down, children name their feelings instead of accusing and agree a fair turn rule, and both feel lighter.

subtype: Stage 1: Public teasing meets a raw spot [Receiver]
passage:
Monday: The unit test marks came out. Ramesh got 41 out of 100 in maths. He folded the sheet into a tiny square and didn't show his father.

Tuesday night: The Class 10 group chat was busy. Pema posted a screenshot of the class list and wrote, "Ramesh topping from the bottom again lol". Three people reacted. Ramesh's stomach dropped. Maybe he really was the dumb one. His thumbs moved before his brain did: "At least I don't copy my homework from my cousin like you, Pema." He hit send in four seconds.

Wednesday: At school, nobody mentioned the marks. Everyone mentioned his reply. Pema looked hurt, and Ramesh felt worse than he had on Monday. He wished he'd just put the phone down.

qa.q: What did Ramesh get in maths?
qa.a: Ramesh got 41 out of 100 in maths.

qa.q: What was Ramesh afraid of when he read Pema's message?
qa.a: He feared he really was the dumb one, so the tease hit a raw spot and he replied instantly because staying silent felt like agreeing.

qa.q: What could Ramesh try next time a message hits a sore spot?
qa.a: He could put the phone down for a few minutes, or tell Pema privately that the joke hurt, instead of firing back in the group.

qa.q: How might Pema see Ramesh's reply?
qa.a: Pema may have thought it was just a joke and felt hurt and embarrassed by the counter-attack in front of the class.

grounding: Over three days a teen teased about his marks in a group chat, touching his fear of not being good enough, replies instantly before thinking.

passage:
Dear Himani,

I need to tell someone who isn't in my class.

You know how Tara and Nisha had that fight over the dance group? It was just the two of them on Monday. By Friday, it's the whole class. Half the girls are "Team Tara," half are "Team Nisha," and they don't even sit together at lunch.

The worst part: people are repeating things said in private. Someone told Nisha that Tara called her "clingy" in a voice note months ago. Now nobody remembers the dance group at all. It's just about which side you're on.

Both sides asked me to choose. I said no, and now both think I'm secretly with the other one. I feel stuck, and sad, because I don't think Tara and Nisha even wanted this.

Tell me what you'd do.

Love,
Leela

qa.q: What did Tara and Nisha first fight over?
qa.a: They fought over the dance group.

qa.q: What is Leela feeling about being asked to choose a side?
qa.a: Leela feels stuck and sad, distrusted by both sides for refusing to choose.

qa.q: What could Leela do next to help, rather than join a camp?
qa.a: Leela could talk to Tara and Nisha separately, suggest they speak to each other directly, and refuse to pass on private messages.

qa.q: How might Nisha feel on hearing the old voice note repeated?
qa.a: Nisha probably felt hurt and betrayed, and more bound to her own camp, with the original quarrel now buried.

grounding: A letter from a classmate shows a two-person quarrel growing into two camps as friends take sides and repeat private words.

"You've been in your room since lunch, Omkar." Jasleen didi leaned on the door frame. "Mummy thinks you're sick."

"I'm not sick."

"Is this still about Aman?"

He threw the pillow at the wall, but softly. "He said I sing like a goat. On stage. At rehearsal."

"And you said?"

"I said his dad can't sing either."

"Omkar."

"I know! It was stupid." He sat up. "I've been angry all day. But I'm not angry at what he said. I'm angry that everyone laughed. Even Kunal."

Jasleen sat on the bed. "That's different."

"Yeah." He rubbed his face. He felt tired, and oddly a bit curious about himself. "How do I fix it without looking like I lost?"

"Maybe it's not about losing," she said. "What would you want Aman to say to you?"

qa.q: What did Aman say about Omkar's singing?
qa.a: He said Omkar sings like a goat.

qa.q: What is Omkar realising about his own feelings?
qa.a: He realises he is more hurt and embarrassed about everyone laughing than about Aman's words, and his anger is draining into tiredness.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Omkar now?
qa.a: He could think about what he'd want to hear from Aman and offer something similar, stepping back without seeing it as losing.

qa.q: How does Jasleen see her brother's situation?
qa.a: Jasleen seems caring and patient, helping Omkar see that fixing things need not mean looking weak.

grounding: After a day of sulking, a teen realises he is more hurt about being laughed at, and wonders how to step back without looking weak.
